name: Sun
description: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star that sits at the centre of our Solar System and provides the energy necessary for life on Earth. Its gravity holds the entire system together, keeping everything from the largest planets to the smallest debris in orbit. As a massive ball of glowing gas, it accounts for more than 99 per cent of the total mass of the Solar System.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) developed and tested the X-ray camera detectors on SMILE, the ESA–CAS mission studying how the solar wind meets Earth’s magnetic field. How particles from the Sun damage detectors in space is one of the CEI’s core research areas, and we test detectors against space radiation for missions across the Solar System.

name: Mercury
description: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest to the Sun, resulting in extreme temperature variations. Its heavily cratered surface resembles Earth's Moon, indicating that the planet has been geologically quiet for billions of years. Despite its small size, it has a global magnetic field, which is surprising for such a small planet, and a high density that suggests a massive metallic core.
ou_involvement: We have studied Mercury’s surface composition for decades, using spectroscopy of data from visiting spacecraft to map its chemical elements and trace the planet’s early volcanic history. Our scientists are Co-Investigators on BepiColombo’s MIXS X-ray spectrometer, which will map the elements on its surface.

name: BepiColombo
description: BepiColombo, a joint ESA-JAXA mission, is due to enter orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026 and to be fully commissioned by April 2027. Its two orbiters will make the most complete study yet of Mercury’s surface, composition and magnetic field, mapping it at many wavelengths to explain the planet’s oversized core and its richness in volatile materials. The model shows the moment JAXA’s Mio orbiter is released; after that, the MOSIF sunshield separates and ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) flies free.
ou_involvement: We were on BepiColombo’s M-CAM monitoring camera team, analysing images from its Mercury flybys, and have led ESA’s Mercury Surface and Composition Working Group. With instrument lead the University of Leicester, we helped build the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Our scientists are now Co-Investigators on MIXS and on MERTIS, the Mercury Thermal Infrared Spectrometer, and associates on SIMBIO-SYS, the orbiter’s imaging and spectrometer system.

name: Venus
description: Venus is often called Earth’s twin due to its similar size and density, but it possesses a thick, toxic atmosphere that creates a runaway greenhouse effect. The planet rotates backwards on its axis and suffers from surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead. Its surface is hidden by thick clouds of sulfuric acid, which are only penetrable by radar and specialised spectrometers.
ou_involvement: We’re helping to prepare ESA’s EnVision mission to Venus. With a £2.3 million ESA grant, our team leads the testing of the detectors in the VenSpec-U ultraviolet spectrometer, which will study the sulphur chemistry of Venus’s clouds, and we take part in the mission’s science preparations.

name: Earth
description: Earth is the only known planet to support life and is characterised by its vast oceans and nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere. It features a dynamic surface shaped by plate tectonics and an active climate system that regulates temperatures for its diverse ecosystems. Our home planet sits within the Sun's habitable zone, allowing water to exist in liquid form on the surface.
ou_involvement: We use Earth observation data to monitor environmental change, developing machine learning to track deforestation, urban growth and glacial retreat in satellite images. The work also feeds our teaching on technology and environmental sustainability.

name: ISS
description: The International Space Station is a modular research laboratory that orbits the Earth and serves as a home for international crews. It provides a unique microgravity environment where scientists can conduct experiments that would be impossible on the ground. The station is a symbol of international cooperation, involving space agencies from the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada.
ou_involvement: Our scientists took part in BIOMEX, a DLR-led experiment outside the ISS that exposed bacteria, algae, lichens and fungi to the vacuum, UV radiation and temperature extremes of space for about 18 months. The samples came home with British astronaut Tim Peake in June 2016, and the results helped show whether such organisms (and, by extension, life on Mars) could survive travelling between planets.

name: Hubble
description: Hubble, a joint NASA/ESA mission, is one of the most successful space telescopes ever built, and has spent over three decades providing iconic images of the deep universe. It orbits above the Earth's atmosphere to capture clear views of galaxies, nebulae, and planets without the distortion caused by our air. The mission has fundamentally changed our understanding of the age of the universe and the existence of dark energy.
ou_involvement: Our astronomers use Hubble’s archive to study stellar populations and how distant galaxies evolve, and the work feeds into our astronomy teaching. The CCDs in Hubble’s WFC3 camera were built by Teledyne e2v, the UK company that partners with our Centre for Electronic Imaging on testing and radiation-hardening space detectors.

name: Sentinel-4
description: Sentinel-4 is a Copernicus mission to monitor air quality over Europe from geostationary orbit, 36,000 km above the equator. Its ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared spectrometer flies on EUMETSAT’s Meteosat Third Generation Sounder satellite (MTG-S1), launched on 1 July 2025, and measures ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, formaldehyde and aerosols every hour.
ou_involvement: [TO ADD: OU involvement, needs input]

name: CASTOR
description: CASTOR is a proposed Canadian-led space telescope designed to perform high-resolution imaging in the ultraviolet and blue-optical wavelengths. It will feature a wide-field view that is significantly larger than Hubble's, enabling it to survey vast portions of the sky. The mission aims to address fundamental questions in cosmology, including the nature of dark energy and the formation of galaxies.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) won £2.1 million to lead the testing and space qualification of the CIS303 and CIS120 UV detectors, built by Teledyne e2v, for CASTOR, a Canadian-led 1-metre UV/optical telescope targeting launch around 2030. We test and optimise the detectors, and measure how well different UV coatings work and how they degrade, to get the sensors ready for spaceflight.

name: Spektr-UV
description: Spektr-UV, also known as the World Space Observatory–Ultraviolet (WSO-UV), is a planned Russian-led space telescope with a 1.7-metre mirror. It will observe at ultraviolet wavelengths, between 115 and 310 nanometres, that are blocked by our atmosphere, taking spectra and images of stars, galaxies and planets. After many delays, it is now expected to launch no earlier than 2031.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) contributed to the detector technology for WSO-UV’s Spectrographs Unit. Its CCD cameras must collect light for up to an hour and read out very faint signals with very little noise, and we studied how radiation damage in orbit would affect the sensors’ ability to do that.

name: TRUTHS
description: TRUTHS is a UK-led mission delivered by ESA that aims to create a 'gold standard' reference point for climate measurements in space. It will measure the Sun's incoming radiation and Earth's reflected radiation with unprecedented accuracy to calibrate other satellites. This high-precision data will significantly increase our confidence in long-term climate change data and environmental forecasting.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) tests how radiation damages the Teledyne e2v CIS120 CMOS sensor, which is being evaluated for TRUTHS and other next-generation missions. We measure its dark current, noise and sensitivity before and after gamma and proton irradiation, at a range of temperatures, to check it can keep the high calibration accuracy TRUTHS needs over a multi-year mission.

name: SMILE
description: The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer is a collaborative mission between ESA and CAS that launched on 19 May 2026. It is designed to provide the first global images of the Earth's magnetosphere and its dynamic interaction with the solar wind. By observing X-ray emissions, the mission aims to reveal how solar activity impacts our planet's magnetic shield and atmosphere.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) developed and tested the twin CCD370 detectors (4,510 × 4,510 pixels, derived from the CCD270s developed for PLATO) at the heart of SMILE’s Soft X-ray Imager. We’re now part of the mission’s operations team, working with the imager’s team to get the most science from the detectors.

name: Swift
description: Swift is a multi-wavelength space observatory dedicated to detecting and localising gamma-ray bursts within seconds. It rapidly reorients itself to observe the afterglow of these massive cosmic explosions across X-ray and optical wavelengths. Over more than 20 years it has transformed our understanding of black hole formation and neutron star mergers. With its orbit decaying faster than expected, a commercial mission to boost it was called off in August 2026, and Swift is expected to re-enter the atmosphere by the end of the year.

name: UKube-1
description: UKube-1 was the first mission commissioned by the UK Space Agency to demonstrate advanced CubeSat technologies in orbit. It served as a way maker for the UK small satellite industry by testing payloads for space weather monitoring and secure communications. The mission provided invaluable hands-on experience for researchers and students across multiple British universities.
ou_involvement: Our Compact CMOS Camera Demonstrator (C3D) won one of only three science payload slots on UKube-1, the UK Space Agency’s first CubeSat. Launched in July 2014, its three cameras made the first in-orbit demonstration of a European 0.18-micron CMOS imaging technology. Radiation testing showed the sensor degrading much like a CCD, along with effects unique to CMOS such as single-event upsets, and the data has since informed the design of more radiation-tolerant space CMOS sensors.

name: AlSat-Nano
description: AlSat-Nano was a joint UK-Algerian mission to build and operate a 3U CubeSat, launched in 2016. The project was designed to train Algerian students, drawing on UK engineering experience.
ou_involvement: We provided AlSat-Nano’s C3D2 camera, a successor to the C3D camera on UKube-1. Its three cameras imaged the Earth, tested commercial camera sensors in space and watched the CubeSat’s AstroTube boom unfold, and it also served as a remote experiment for our students in the Open Science Laboratory.

name: Moon
description: Since its formation 4.5 billion years ago, the Moon has been our nearest neighbour in space. Its cratered surface preserves a historical record of the near-Earth environment long since lost on our home planet. The Moon influences our planet's tides and rotational stability, our culture and our scientific understanding of our place in the Universe. It is the only celestial body that humans have visited, and is widely regarded as a potential stepping stone into deep space.
ou_involvement: Our analysis of Apollo samples helped show that the Moon is not as dry as once thought: water is locked inside lunar minerals. Drawing on instruments we built for Beagle 2 and Rosetta, we now develop miniature laboratories to measure what the Moon is made of. We also study how lunar soil could supply water, oxygen and fuel, and be used to build on the Moon, to support sustainable exploration.

name: Chandrayaan-1
description: Chandrayaan-1 was India's first lunar probe and was instrumental in discovering widespread evidence of water molecules on the Moon. It carried a suite of international instruments to create a detailed three-dimensional map of the lunar surface and its mineral composition. The mission successfully reached lunar orbit and operated for nearly a year before its mission was completed.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) assessed how protons would damage the 24 CCD54 X-ray detectors in the C1XS instrument, modelling the shielding, temperature and voltages they needed. We tested 14 candidate detector modules before launch, recommended the ten best for flight, and advised on how the detectors coped with radiation in orbit.

name: Chandrayaan-2
description: Chandrayaan-2 is India’s second mission to the Moon, launched in July 2019. Its lander, Vikram, crashed during its descent that September, but the orbiter has been mapping the Moon ever since from a polar orbit about 100 km up, studying its surface, its minerals and the elements it is made of.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) helped prepare the CCD236 X-ray detectors in the orbiter’s CLASS spectrometer, the successor to Chandrayaan-1’s C1XS, which maps the elements in the Moon’s surface. We characterised the detectors and tested them against radiation, and by finding the best temperatures, readout speeds and voltages we doubled their resistance to radiation damage.

name: Chang'e-5
description: Chang'e-5 was a landmark Chinese mission that successfully returned approximately two kilograms of lunar soil and rocks to Earth in late 2020. It targeted a younger region of the Moon called Oceanus Procellarum to provide insights into late-stage lunar volcanic activity. The mission involved a complex series of manoeuvres, including an automated docking in lunar orbit for the return journey.
ou_involvement: In April 2025 we became one of only seven institutions outside China chosen to borrow Chang’e-5 samples. In our laboratories we’re measuring the isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and noble gases in the grains, to test the giant-impact theory of the Moon’s origin and trace the history of volatiles in the Earth-Moon system.

name: PROSPECT
description: PROSPECT is the European Space Agency's exploration science payload for finding and analysing water ice and other materials on the Moon. An Italian drill collects samples from up to a metre below the surface, for analysis in the OU-provided ProSPA instrument. The package will be delivered to a south polar region of the Moon by the Intuitive Machines IM-4 lander, planned for 2027.
ou_involvement: We lead the design and development of ProSPA, a miniature laboratory that will analyse samples on the Moon itself. It heats lunar soil just as meteorites and returned samples are analysed in laboratories on Earth, and its mass spectrometers identify, measure and isotopically characterise water ice and other volatiles.

name: LUPEX
description: LUPEX is a joint JAXA-ISRO mission to look for water and other resources at the Moon’s south pole. Due to launch no earlier than 2028, its rover will explore sites with different lighting, temperatures and geology, measuring how much water there is, where, and in what form, down to about 1.5 metres. It should work for about 3.5 months after landing, and possibly for up to a year.
ou_involvement: We’re developing EMS-L, the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer for LUPEX, an ESA instrument on the JAXA-ISRO rover. Building on our heritage in miniature ion-trap mass spectrometry, it will measure water and other volatiles in the thin lunar exosphere and those released as the rover drives and drills, to show how volatiles are spread and behave at the Moon’s south pole.

name: MAGPIE
description: MAGPIE is ESA's first lunar rover, designed to operate for up to 10 Earth days at the lunar south pole, where it will drill into the subsurface to analyse material for water and other volatiles. The rover is being built by ispace Europe and is due to fly on ispace’s Mission 4 lander in 2029.
ou_involvement: We’re developing the Volatile Analyser, the ion-trap mass spectrometer in the Lunar Volatiles Scout drill on ESA’s MAGPIE rover. Building on our heritage in ion-trap mass spectrometry, it will identify and measure water and other volatiles in lunar soil, and how they vary with depth at the Moon’s south pole.

name: Shackleton Rover
description: Taking inspiration from Sir Ernest Shackleton's 1914 expedition, and in coordination with his family, Shackleton Rover is a proposed UK-led mission to the lunar south pole. It would showcase and develop the UK's technological, scientific and industrial capabilities in space exploration while inspiring the next generation of space scientists and engineers. By establishing a long-lived experiment on the Moon, it would also give the UK a voice in the responsible exploration of the Moon and its resources.
ou_involvement: We’re helping to define the payload and the mission for Shackleton Rover, a concept for a rover system for the lunar south pole that would be built and operated entirely in the UK.

name: Earth-Sun L2
description: Lagrange Point 2 is a point where the pull of the Sun and Earth balances a spacecraft's orbital motion, located approximately 1.5 million kilometres away from the Earth, directly opposite the Sun. It provides a perfect, quiet environment for space telescopes to observe the deep universe without interference from Earth's heat. Spacecraft at this location follow a halo or Lissajous orbit to maintain a constant line of sight for communication.
ou_involvement: We treat L2 as a natural laboratory for how deep space affects spacecraft components, following the performance of detectors we characterised for missions stationed there. What we learn improves the detectors we’re developing for future flagship missions.

name: JWST
description: The James Webb Space Telescope is the premier space observatory of the decade, designed to solve mysteries in our solar system and beyond. It uses a massive gold-coated mirror to capture faint infrared light from the very first stars and galaxies formed after the Big Bang. Since its launch in 2021, it has revolutionised our understanding of exoplanet atmospheres and galactic evolution.
ou_involvement: Our astronomers use JWST to study the atmospheres of planets around other stars. We were part of the international teams that analysed JWST’s first detailed observations of the giant planet WASP-39b, revealing its clouds and chemistry, and research we funded has studied the small rocky planet L 98-59 d, where JWST found possible signs of volcanic gases.

name: Gaia
description: Gaia is an ambitious ESA mission designed to create the largest and most precise three-dimensional map of our galaxy. By surveying nearly two billion stars, it provides data on their positions, distances, and motions with incredible accuracy. This massive dataset allows astronomers to reconstruct the history and future of the Milky Way across billions of years.
ou_involvement: Before launch, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) modelled how radiation damage would trap charge in Gaia’s CCDs, and we’ve since analysed its in-flight radiation data for the mission’s data processing. Gaia’s detectors turned out less damaged than ground tests predicted, a puzzle we’re still investigating to improve how future missions are tested. Our PhD students use Gaia’s catalogues to study star clusters and binary stars, our researchers use its alerts to find transient objects, and students on our S818 Space Science module follow up Gaia targets with our remote telescope in Tenerife.

name: Euclid
description: Euclid is an ESA space telescope designed to investigate the 'Dark Universe' by observing the shapes and distances of billions of galaxies. It maps the structure of the cosmos out to 10 billion light-years to track how dark matter and dark energy influence the expansion of the universe. The mission provides high-resolution imaging that allows scientists to detect the subtle effects of gravitational lensing.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) played a lead role in characterising the CCD273 detectors in Euclid’s VIS instrument, and developed ‘trap pumping’, now used in orbit. It pinpoints individual radiation-damage defects in the detectors to within a fraction of a pixel, so images can be corrected and kept precise enough to trace dark matter through gravitational lensing. Our astronomers also lead searches of Euclid’s surveys for rare gravitational lenses.

name: NewAthena
description: NewAthena is a planned ESA X-ray observatory, due for launch in 2037, designed to answer fundamental questions about the 'Hot and Energetic Universe.' It will observe massive black holes, galaxy clusters, and the hot gas that fills the space between galaxies to see how they evolve over time. The telescope will feature a massive collecting area and high-spectral resolution to detect the movement of matter under extreme gravity.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) is working with partners worldwide to design and test graded-Z shielding for NewAthena’s Wide Field Imager: layers of heavy and light materials that block high-energy particles and the secondary radiation they produce. We model how the shielding will perform in orbit with the GEANT4 toolkit, checked against real detector tests.

name: HWO
description: The Habitable Worlds Observatory is a future flagship NASA telescope designed to find and characterise Earth-like planets around other stars. It will use a massive, stable mirror and a coronagraph to block out starlight, allowing it to image faint planets in the habitable zone. The mission's primary goal is to search for biosignatures like oxygen and methane in the atmospheres of distant worlds.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) is developing low-noise UV and photon-counting detectors for HWO’s faint imaging, building on our CASTOR work. We’re also part of the UK consortium awarded £3 million in 2026 to develop one of the telescope’s core instruments.

name: PLATO
description: PLATO is an upcoming ESA mission designed to detect and characterise Earth-sized exoplanets orbiting bright, Sun-like stars. It will use 26 separate cameras to monitor hundreds of thousands of stars for the tiny dip in brightness caused by a planet passing in front. The mission aims to find worlds in the habitable zone where liquid water could exist on the surface.
ou_involvement: We lead population studies, funded by the UK Space Agency, to weed out false positives such as blended eclipsing binaries that could be mistaken for planets in PLATO’s fields. Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) also works on the detectors’ performance, calibration and radiation tolerance, and our robotic telescopes could follow up candidate stars once PLATO is flying.

name: Roman
description: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched on 30 August 2026, will provide a field of view 100 times larger than Hubble's while maintaining the same high-resolution quality. It is designed to perform massive surveys that will help scientists understand dark energy and the distribution of exoplanets in our galaxy. The mission also carries a technology demonstration coronagraph to test new ways of directly imaging planets around other stars.
ou_involvement: From 2014 to 2019, under contract to JPL, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) characterised, designed and tested the EM-CCD sensor for Roman’s coronagraph, leading to the CCD311 chosen for flight: a radiation-hardened version of the CCD201. We continue to refine the ‘trap-pumping’ techniques we developed for Euclid to counter radiation damage to these sensors.

name: Mars
description: Mars is known as the Red Planet due to the iron oxide on its surface and features the largest volcanoes and deepest canyons in the Solar System. Its thin atmosphere and frozen polar caps suggest a world that was once much warmer and wetter billions of years ago. Today, it is the focus of intense robotic exploration as scientists look for signs of ancient microbial life.
ou_involvement: We have a long history of Mars research, from building lander instruments to analysing atmospheric data from orbit. Our researchers study the planet’s volatile cycles and whether its subsurface could be habitable, and help space agencies choose landing sites, as for the Rosalind Franklin rover at Oxia Planum.

name: ExoMars TGO
description: The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter is an ESA-led mission designed to map the presence of trace gases, like methane, in the Martian atmosphere. It orbits the planet to identify potential biological or geological sources of these gases while studying the atmosphere's composition and structure. The orbiter also serves as a vital communications relay for rovers on the surface, including NASA's Perseverance and Curiosity.
ou_involvement: We designed and led the development of UVIS, the ultraviolet channel of TGO’s NOMAD spectrometer, and one of our planetary scientists is a Co-Principal Investigator for NOMAD. We also help operate the CaSSIS stereo camera. We use UVIS data to track ozone, water vapour and trace gases such as methane, to understand how Mars loses its water to space. Some measurements are timed with other spacecraft: TGO measures methane from orbit while Curiosity measures it on the ground.

name: Schiaparelli
description: Schiaparelli was ESA's Entry, Descent and Landing Demonstrator Module, carried to Mars with the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2016. It returned data throughout its descent through the Martian atmosphere, but a fault in its guidance software ended its parachute phase too early, and it crashed onto Meridiani Planum on 19 October 2016.
ou_involvement: We co-led AMELIA, the team that used Schiaparelli’s entry and descent data to reconstruct the Martian atmosphere it flew through, measuring its density, pressure and temperature from higher up than ever before.

name: I-MIM
description: The International Mars Ice Mapper (I-MIM) is a proposed orbiter, planned by the space agencies of Canada, the USA, Japan, Italy and the Netherlands, that would use radar to map water ice buried near the surface of Mars and help choose landing sites for future human missions.
ou_involvement: We’re developing a combined visible-infrared imager, with a detector made by Teledyne e2v, for future Mars missions such as I-MIM and ESA’s LightShip-1. It can tell water ice from carbon dioxide ice on the surface, and in December 2025 the UK Space Agency awarded us £1.2 million for the next phase.

name: Beagle 2
description: Beagle 2 was a UK-led Mars lander that was deployed from the Mars Express spacecraft in 2003 but failed to transmit data after landing. The spacecraft was thought to be lost until 2015, when high-resolution images from NASA's MRO showed the lander had partially deployed on the Martian surface. It was designed to search for signs of past life by analysing the isotopic composition of carbon in Martian rocks.
ou_involvement: Beagle 2 was conceived and led by our own Colin Pillinger, and we designed its Gas Analysis Package (GAP): a miniaturised mass spectrometer with twelve ovens, built to detect isotopic signs of past life in Martian soil. Fitting a laboratory-scale instrument into a probe the size of a dinner plate took major feats of miniaturisation. Our scientists also worked on its Environmental Sensor Suite, which was to measure the weather and look for dust devils. Contact was lost after the 2003 landing, but the lessons learned informed later landers, including ExoMars.

name: Perseverance
description: Perseverance is NASA's most advanced Mars rover and is currently exploring the Jezero Crater for signs of ancient microbial life. It is equipped with a sophisticated drill and a sample caching system to collect and store Martian rocks for a future return to Earth. The rover also carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which demonstrated the first powered flight on another planet.
ou_involvement: Our researchers were on the NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return Campaign Science Group and worked on planetary protection, planning how best to bring Perseverance’s Jezero Crater samples to Earth and analyse them. We also use the rover’s images and remote sensing to study the minerals of the ancient river delta, including clays and carbonates formed by water, and share this research with our students.

name: ExoMars Rosalind Franklin
description: The Rosalind Franklin rover is a major ESA mission designed to search for signs of life in the Martian subsurface at Oxia Planum. It features a unique drill that can reach up to two metres underground to collect samples protected from harsh surface radiation. The rover will carry a suite of scientific instruments to analyse the geology, mineralogy, and chemistry of these ancient samples.
ou_involvement: We’re on the Rosalind Franklin rover’s science team: as deputy principal investigator for its PanCam camera system, as one of the UK’s Interdisciplinary Scientists, and in support of PanCam and the Enfys spectrometer. We’re also leading and contributing to preparations through operations simulations and field trials.

name: MSL Curiosity
description: The Mars Science Laboratory, known as Curiosity, is a car-sized rover that has been exploring Gale Crater since 2012, recently passing 5,000 sols (Martian days) on the surface. Its primary goal is to determine if Mars ever had an environment capable of supporting microbial life by studying its geology and climate. The mission has successfully identified evidence of ancient freshwater lakes and complex organic molecules on the Martian surface.
ou_involvement: Our academics are on Curiosity’s science and operations teams, focusing on noble gases and on how Martian rocks reacted with ancient water, which bears on whether Mars was habitable. Others combine the rover’s weather data with ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter observations to model Mars’s dust and water cycles.

name: Phobos
description: Phobos is the larger and inner of Mars’s two small moons, an irregular lump about 26 by 23 by 18 kilometres. It circles Mars only about 6,000 kilometres above the surface, closer to its planet than any other known moon, three times a day: faster than Mars turns, so from the ground it rises in the west. Tides are slowly drawing it in, and in some tens of millions of years it will break apart or crash into Mars. Its dark surface is scarred by Stickney, a crater 9 kilometres wide, and by long parallel grooves. Whether Phobos and Deimos are captured asteroids or formed from debris thrown off Mars by a giant impact is still debated, and JAXA’s MMX mission is to bring a sample of Phobos back to Earth to help settle it. The model shown is NASA’s.

name: Deimos
description: Deimos is the smaller and outer of Mars’s two moons, about 16 by 12 by 10 kilometres. It orbits about 23,500 kilometres from the centre of Mars every 30 hours, only a little slower than Mars turns, so from the surface it creeps across the sky and stays up for more than two days at a time. Its surface is smoother than Phobos’s, its craters softened by a thick layer of fine dust. JAXA’s MMX mission is to study it during flybys. The model shown is NASA’s.

name: Jupiter
description: Jupiter is the largest planet in our Solar System and is a massive gas giant famous for its Great Red Spot. It has about a hundred known moons and a faint ring system, serving as a miniature solar system for astronomers to study. Its intense gravity and magnetic field have a profound influence on the movement of objects throughout the outer Solar System.

name: Io
description: Io is the innermost of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons and is the most geologically active body in the Solar System. Its surface is constantly reshaped by hundreds of volcanoes, which are fuelled by the intense tidal heating caused by Jupiter's gravity. The moon's yellow-orange colour is a result of the sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost that covers its entire surface.

name: Europa
description: Europa is an icy moon of Jupiter that is believed to hide a massive liquid water ocean beneath its frozen crust. Its smooth surface is crisscrossed by cracks and streaks, suggesting that the ice shell is dynamic and relatively young. Scientists consider Europa one of the best candidates in the Solar System for finding habitable environments beyond Earth.
ou_involvement: Our astrobiologists study Europa as one of the Solar System’s most promising ocean worlds. We develop new cryogenic laboratory techniques and simulation facilities to study icy surface materials down to the microscale, and our fieldwork in polar places such as the Canadian High Arctic shows how ice and salts brought to the surface by cryovolcanism can reveal conditions in the ocean far below. We also model how the ocean’s chemistry, and how habitable it is, may have changed over 4.5 billion years as the water reacted with the rock beneath.

name: Ganymede
description: Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and is even bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the only known moon to possess its own magnetic field, which creates brilliant aurorae around its poles. The moon features a mix of dark, cratered regions and lighter, grooved terrain that indicates a complex geological history.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) helped develop and tested the image sensor in JANUS, the camera on ESA’s JUICE mission, which will study Ganymede from orbit.

name: Callisto
description: Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in the Solar System and shows very few signs of geological activity on its ancient surface. It is composed of equal parts rock and ice and may also contain a subsurface ocean deep within its interior. Its distance from Jupiter means it is less affected by the planet's intense radiation environment compared to the other Galilean moons.

name: JUICE
description: The JUpiter ICy moons Explorer is a major ESA mission launched in 2023 to investigate the habitability of Jupiter's large moons. It is currently cruising through the solar system and will arrive at Jupiter in 2031 to perform detailed studies of Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto. The mission aims to understand how habitable environments could arise around gas giant planets in the outer Solar System.
ou_involvement: Working with Teledyne e2v, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) helped develop and characterise the CIS115 sensor at the heart of the JANUS camera, testing it against the radiation, vibration and temperature extremes of the journey to Jupiter. We are the UK National Lead for JANUS.

name: Saturn
description: Saturn is a massive gas giant famous for its spectacular ring system, which is composed primarily of ice and rock particles. It is the second-largest planet in the Solar System and has a diverse collection of hundreds of moons, including the massive, orange-hued Titan. Despite its great size, the planet has a very low density and would theoretically float if placed in a large enough ocean.
ou_involvement: We helped calibrate Cassini’s Cosmic Dust Analyser and studied the composition of dust around Saturn. One of our scientists, John Zarnecki, led the Surface Science Package on the Huygens probe, which landed on Titan, Saturn’s largest moon.

name: Titan
description: Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and the only moon in the Solar System to possess a thick atmosphere and liquid lakes on its surface. These lakes are composed of liquid methane and ethane, creating a weather cycle similar to Earth's but at much colder temperatures. Its thick, orange haze hides a complex surface that features vast dunes, mountains, and potentially even cryovolcanoes.
ou_involvement: Titan’s first global geomorphological map, published in Nature Astronomy in 2019, used Cassini data to identify six major terrain types, from plains to dune fields. Our astrobiologists study Titan as one of the icy ocean worlds, exploring how its surface chemistry and methane cycle relate to conditions for life.

name: Enceladus
description: Enceladus is a small, bright icy moon of Saturn, about 500 km across. Jets of water vapour and ice grains erupt from cracks near its south pole, fed by a salty ocean beneath its icy crust, and the Cassini spacecraft sampled them by flying through the plume. Its ocean contains many of the ingredients thought to be needed for life, making it a prime target in the search for habitable worlds.
ou_involvement: One of our planetary scientists sat on ESA’s Expert Committee that, in 2024, recommended Enceladus as the target of ESA’s next large mission: an orbiter and lander to search for signs of life, for launch in the early 2040s.

name: Cassini
description: The Cassini-Huygens mission was a landmark international collaboration that spent 13 years exploring the Saturnian system in incredible detail. It discovered active geysers on the moon Enceladus and provided our first clear views of Titan's surface through its thick atmosphere. The mission concluded in 2017 with a deliberate plunge into Saturn's atmosphere to protect its moons from contamination.
ou_involvement: Our planetary scientists use Cassini’s datasets to study the habitability and chemistry of Saturn’s icy moons. We helped calibrate its Cosmic Dust Analyser and studied the dust around Saturn, and we still use Cassini’s archive to train students in planetary science.

name: Huygens
description: The Huygens probe was an ESA spacecraft that performed the first and only landing in the outer Solar System on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. It successfully transmitted data and images during its two-hour descent through the moon's thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere. The landing revealed a world of riverbeds and rounded pebbles that were shaped by the flow of liquid methane.
ou_involvement: One of our scientists, John Zarnecki, was Principal Investigator for the Surface Science Package (SSP), which made the first measurements on Titan’s surface: its density, temperature and physical state as Huygens landed. We have continued to lead analysis of this unique dataset to understand Titan’s surface and organic chemistry.

name: Uranus
description: Uranus is an ice giant planet that is uniquely characterised by its extreme axial tilt, causing it to rotate almost on its side. Its pale blue-green colour is a result of the methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red light and reflects blue and green. It features a faint ring system and a diverse family of 29 known moons, most of which are composed of ice and rock.

name: Rosetta
description: ESA’s Rosetta made the first long-term study of a comet’s nucleus, orbiting Comet 67P for over two years as it travelled through the inner Solar System. Its lander, Philae, studied the surface directly, giving ground truth for the orbiter’s measurements. Together they revealed the physical and chemical make-up of comets and their possible part in the origin of life.
ou_involvement: With RAL Space, we co-developed Ptolemy, the gas analyser on the Philae lander that measured the isotopes of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen in the comet. We also contributed to the MUPUS and GIADA instruments, coordinated the mission’s worldwide campaign of ground-based observations, and have explored why comet 67P’s dust and gas jets follow a day-night cycle.

name: Philae
description: Philae was the robotic lander carried by the Rosetta spacecraft and became the first mission to land successfully on a comet's nucleus in 2014. It carried a suite of ten instruments designed to perform in-situ analysis of the comet's surface and subsurface materials. Despite a bounce during landing, it successfully transmitted data back to Earth before entering hibernation.
ou_involvement: With RAL Space, we designed and built the Ptolemy gas analyser, which with the COSAC instrument made the first analysis of organic matter on a comet’s surface. Our academics lead the interpretation of its data in the search for life’s chemical building blocks, work that has made our name in miniature planetary laboratories and comet science.

name: Hera
description: Hera is an ESA planetary defence mission launched in 2024 to investigate the binary asteroid system Didymos and its moon Dimorphos. It will study the results of NASA's DART mission, which successfully impacted Dimorphos to demonstrate a kinetic deflection technique. The spacecraft will characterise the crater and the asteroid's internal structure to help refine our planetary defence strategies.
ou_involvement: Our researchers were on the Hera Science Team’s management board.

name: DART
description: NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was the first test of planetary defence by changing an asteroid's path. Launched in November 2021, it deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, on 26 September 2022, shortening its orbit by about 33 minutes. ESA's Hera mission was sent to study the aftermath.
ou_involvement: Our planetary scientists helped study the aftermath of the impact from the ground, using the MUSE spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope to follow the cloud of debris thrown off Dimorphos over the following month, mapping its cone, spirals, clumps and tails.

name: AKARI
description: AKARI was a Japanese infrared astronomy satellite that performed an all-sky survey at various infrared wavelengths. It was designed to study the formation and evolution of stars and galaxies across the history of the universe. The mission produced high-quality catalogues that continue to be a vital resource for astronomers worldwide.
ou_involvement: We were one of the international partners on JAXA’s AKARI infrared satellite, alongside Nagoya University, the University of Tokyo, ESA and other UK institutions. We used its all-sky infrared survey and spectra to study interstellar dust, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and the earliest star formation in galaxies: part of the cosmic chemical cycle that eventually leads to habitable worlds.

name: Hitomi
description: Hitomi (ASTRO-H) was JAXA’s X-ray observatory, built with NASA and international partners to study the hottest, most energetic places in the universe: galaxy clusters, black holes and the remains of exploded stars. It launched on 17 February 2016 into an orbit about 575 km up, but on 26 March a fault in its attitude control set it spinning and its solar arrays broke away. In its one month of observations it measured the motion of the hot gas in the Perseus galaxy cluster more precisely than ever before. Its successor, XRISM, launched in 2023.
ou_involvement: Researchers at our Centre for Electronic Imaging characterised the p-channel CCDs used in Hitomi’s Soft X-ray Imager, a camera of four CCDs that imaged X-rays from 0.4 to 12 keV across a patch of sky wider than the full Moon.

name: Spitzer
description: The Spitzer Space Telescope was one of NASA's Great Observatories and was optimised for observing the infrared universe. It made numerous high-profile discoveries, including the detection of the TRAPPIST-1 system's Earth-sized exoplanets. The mission operated for over 16 years, providing our clearest views of planet-forming disks and distant, dusty galaxies.
ou_involvement: Our scientists analyse Spitzer’s archived light curves to study the atmospheres and orbits of transiting exoplanets, and use the data to teach infrared astronomy and the search for habitable worlds. The work also helps choose targets for new missions such as Ariel.

name: Herschel
description: Herschel was the largest infrared telescope launched until JWST and was designed to study the coolest objects in the universe. It observed the formation of stars and galaxies across cosmic time and provided our first clear detection of water molecules in star-forming regions. The mission's huge mirror and sensitive detectors allowed it to peer through dust that blocks visible light.
ou_involvement: Our astronomers used data from SPIRE, the camera and spectrometer built for Herschel by an international consortium led by Cardiff University, to study distant galaxies at sub-millimetre wavelengths and trace the history of star formation.

name: Planck
description: The Planck mission was an ESA satellite designed to map the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) with unprecedented precision. It captured the oldest light in the universe, providing a detailed 'baby picture' of the cosmos just 380,000 years after the Big Bang. The mission's data has been essential for refining our understanding of the universe's age, composition, and expansion rate.
ou_involvement: We use Planck’s maps of the cosmic microwave background to study the large-scale structure of the early Universe and how galaxy clusters are spread. Our cosmologists combine Planck’s data with newer missions such as Euclid to research dark matter and dark energy, and it underpins our teaching of cosmology.

name: Peregrine
description: Peregrine-1 was developed by Astrobotic under NASA's Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services programmes. Launched in 2024, it aimed to be the first commercially developed spacecraft to land on the Moon. However, a propulsion system fault after launch ruled out a landing attempt, and instead the spacecraft was operated as a test flight for a week before a controlled disposal in Earth's atmosphere.
ou_involvement: We proposed and developed the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer (EMS), Europe’s contribution to NASA’s PITMS instrument, with ESA funding and RAL Space, on a fast track to meet a tight budget and timescale. It was built to measure the Moon’s thin exosphere and how it changes over the lunar day and with the lander’s own effects. When Peregrine couldn’t land, we ran EMS in space to help diagnose the spacecraft, proving the technology ready to fly again on PROSPECT.

name: Comet Interceptor
description: Comet Interceptor is a unique ESA mission designed to 'ambush' a pristine comet that is entering the inner Solar System for the first time. It will wait at the Earth-Sun L2 point for a suitable target to be discovered by new surveys before being deployed to perform a flyby. The mission aims to study a comet that has never been altered by the Sun's heat, providing a clear look at early Solar System material.
ou_involvement: We’re a Co-Investigator institution for DISC, the instrument that will measure the size, mass and speed of dust particles as the spacecraft flies past its comet. Our Light-Gas Gun fires particles at several kilometres per second to check DISC’s dust shield can survive real high-speed impacts.

name: EnVision
description: EnVision is a planned ESA orbiter mission designed to provide a comprehensive look at Venus' surface geology and atmospheric dynamics. It will feature high-resolution radar and specialised spectrometers to see through the planet's thick clouds and search for signs of active volcanism. The mission aims to determine if Venus was once a habitable planet with liquid water oceans and plate tectonics.
ou_involvement: Our Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group leads the testing of the UV detectors for VenSpec-U, part of EnVision’s VenSpec suite, with a £2.3 million ESA grant. We also take part in the mission’s science preparations ahead of its launch in the early 2030s.

name: LightShip-1
description: ESA’s LightShip-1 is an innovative electric-propulsion tug designed to deliver spacecraft directly into Mars orbit. Once its primary delivery mission is complete, the spacecraft will establish the Mars Communication and Navigation Infrastructure (MARCONI) while also engaging in exploration science through its onboard instruments.
ou_involvement: Our Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group is leading the design phase of HiRIME, the High-Resolution Imager for Mars Exploration, which will take detailed images of the Martian surface for geology. The same group also leads the Dust Environment Spectral Imager, which will image the whole of Mars about every 10 minutes to watch its atmosphere and dust storms.

name: MMX
description: Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) is a JAXA mission to Mars’s two moons, Phobos and Deimos, due to launch in October 2026 and reach Mars about a year later. It will study both moons from close by, land on Phobos to collect at least 10 grams of its surface and bring the sample back to Earth in 2031, to help settle whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars. It also carries IDEFIX, a small French-German rover that will drive on Phobos.
ou_involvement: One of our planetary scientists is on MMX’s science team. In 2023 ESA chose nine European scientists to join the mission’s Science Strategy Teams, and ours is the member for Mars science.

name: OGRE
description: The Off-plane Grating Rocket Experiment is a sub-orbital sounding rocket mission designed to capture the highest-resolution X-ray spectra of stellar sources. It will be launched from a rocket to fly above the Earth's atmosphere for several minutes of precise observations before returning to the ground. The mission aims to study the hot and energetic gas around stars and galaxies to understand their chemical evolution.
ou_involvement: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) characterises and optimises the four EM-CCD sensors in OGRE’s X-ray camera, built by the UK company XCAM to survive the violent vibrations of launch. We research radiation damage, charge transfer and photon counting with these fast detectors for soft X-ray astronomy.

name: Hayabusa2
description: Hayabusa2 was a Japanese mission that successfully deployed multiple rovers and returned samples from the near-Earth asteroid Ryugu. It used a series of innovative techniques, including a kinetic impactor, to collect material from both the surface and subsurface of the asteroid. The mission provided invaluable insights into the composition of carbon-rich asteroids and the history of the early Solar System. The spacecraft is now on an extended mission: it flew past asteroid Torifune on 5 July 2026 and is due to reach the tiny asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031.
ou_involvement: Our oxygen isotope laboratory was invited to join "Team Kochi", one of three Japanese-led teams that made the first analyses of the Ryugu samples. We’re measuring oxygen isotopes in the grains, showing that Ryugu-like material may have delivered water to the early Earth.

name: OSIRIS-REx
description: OSIRIS-REx was a NASA mission that successfully collected a massive sample of rocks and dust from the carbon-rich asteroid Bennu. It returned the samples to Earth in late 2023, providing scientists with pristine material that dates back to the very beginning of our Solar System. The spacecraft has since been renamed OSIRIS-APEX and is now on a new mission to study the asteroid Apophis in 2029.
ou_involvement: We worked with the OSIRIS-REx team to help choose Bennu’s Nightingale sample site, predicting surface temperatures so the spacecraft and samples wouldn’t overheat during collection. We’re also analysing the returned Bennu material to learn about the early Solar System’s chemistry and the origin of Earth’s water and organic molecules.

name: Stardust
description: Stardust was the first mission designed to collect and return samples from a comet's coma and interstellar dust to Earth. It used a unique silica aerogel collector to capture the tiny particles at high speeds without destroying them during the encounter. The mission's return capsule successfully landed in 2006, providing the first clear look at cometary material in a laboratory.
ou_involvement: We were among the first in the world to analyse material from Stardust, using infrared, UV/visible and Raman spectroscopy to study the minerals in dust grains captured from Comet Wild 2 in aerogel. With studies of the samples’ organic content, this work made us a leading UK centre for comet sample science.

name: Bennu
description: Bennu is a diamond-shaped, carbon-rich near-Earth asteroid that is believed to contain primitive material from the birth of our Solar System. Its surface is covered in loose rocks and dust, suggesting it is a 'rubble pile' held together by very weak gravity. The asteroid is a primary target for scientists who are looking to understand the role of asteroids in delivering life's building blocks to Earth.
ou_involvement: We helped choose where OSIRIS-REx sampled Bennu, and we’re analysing the material it brought back to Earth (see OSIRIS-REx).

name: Ryugu
description: Ryugu is a dark, diamond-shaped asteroid that has an orbit that crosses Earth's and is composed primarily of carbon-rich material. Its low density and porous structure indicate that it is a rubble-pile asteroid with significant void spaces in its interior. The asteroid's surface features a mix of large boulders and fine dust, recording a complex history of impacts and space weathering.
ou_involvement: Our oxygen isotope laboratory is one of the international groups analysing Ryugu samples returned by JAXA’s Hayabusa2 (see Hayabusa2).

name: Itokawa
description: Itokawa is a small, peanut-shaped near-Earth asteroid about 535 metres long, named after Hideo Itokawa, the father of Japanese rocketry. In 2005 it was visited by JAXA's Hayabusa spacecraft, which in 2010 brought back the first samples ever collected from an asteroid. Its surface of boulders and gravel suggests it is a rubble pile, reassembled from the fragments of an earlier collision. The shape shown is Robert Gaskell’s model from Hayabusa’s images.
ou_involvement: We analysed particles of Itokawa returned by Hayabusa, carrying out the first Raman spectroscopy on the grains we were allocated. With a team led by Royal Holloway, University of London, we found water and organic matter of extraterrestrial origin in one of them.

name: Phaethon
description: (3200) Phaethon is an unusual asteroid about 6 km across: it approaches the Sun more closely than any other named asteroid, to 0.14 AU (21 million km), well inside Mercury’s orbit. During these passages it behaves like a comet, brightening and developing a dust tail. It is also the parent body of the Geminid meteor shower. Phaethon has occupied this near-Sun orbit for more than 20,000 years and continues to emit gas but little dust, which is puzzling because its surface should long since have been dehydrated and rendered inactive. JAXA’s DESTINY⁺ mission is due to fly past it in 2030.
ou_involvement: Phaethon was discovered by Simon Green, now Emeritus Professor at the OU, and John K. Davies, both then at the University of Leicester. They found it on 11 October 1983 in images from the IRAS infrared satellite: the first asteroid ever discovered in images taken from a spacecraft. Asteroid 9831 SimonGreen is named after him. Today OU researchers are on the DESTINY⁺ team, preparing to interpret the dust it will collect as it flies past Phaethon.

name: DESTINY+
description: DESTINY⁺ (Demonstration and Experiment of Space Technology for INterplanetary voYage, Phaethon fLyby and dUst Science) is a JAXA mission due to launch in 2028 and perform a close flyby of asteroid Phaethon in November 2030. Phaethon still emits gas, and there is no clear evidence of significant surface renewal through ongoing major dust release, making its continued activity an outstanding mystery. The spacecraft will fly past Phaethon at high speed, imaging the body with two cameras and analysing dust released from its surface using impact ionisation mass spectrometry. The mission will also observe several other asteroids, one before and several after its encounter with Phaethon.
ou_involvement: Some OU researchers are members of the DESTINY⁺ Dust Analyzer Instrument Team and part of the DESTINY⁺ Science Working Team. Our work centres on the mission’s core scientific challenge of interpreting the flyby impact ionisation mass spectrometry data that the DDA will return. To build the reference datasets needed for that interpretation, we are carrying out experimental cyclic heating of meteorites considered the best-match to Phaethon, subjecting them to thermal regimes that mimic the extreme heating conditions the asteroid experiences during its perihelion approach. The resulting data allow us to characterise what materials we expect Phaethon to be shedding and to test that expectation directly against the flyby measurements.

name: Hayabusa
description: Hayabusa was a JAXA mission that launched in 2003 and reached the near-Earth asteroid Itokawa in 2005. Despite many technical setbacks, it returned a capsule containing tiny grains of the asteroid to Earth in 2010: the first asteroid samples ever brought back.
ou_involvement: We study grains of Itokawa returned by Hayabusa (see Itokawa).

name: Didymos
description: Didymos is a near-Earth asteroid about 800 metres across, shaped like a spinning top, that turns once every 2.26 hours. It has a small moon, Dimorphos. In September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, the first test of moving an asteroid. ESA's Hera mission arrives in late 2026 to measure exactly what the impact did. The shapes shown here are the models DART's team built from the spacecraft's images.

name: Dimorphos
description: Dimorphos is Didymos's small moon, about 177 metres across, circling it about 1.1 kilometres away every 11 hours 22 minutes. On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft hit it at about 6 kilometres per second, shortening its orbit by about 33 minutes and throwing out a long trail of debris. Before the impact it kept the same face towards Didymos; Hera will find out whether the impact has left it wobbling. The shape shown is DART's model from the images taken in the spacecraft's final minutes.

name: Comet Wild 2
description: Comet Wild 2 is a periodic comet that features a lumpy, cratered nucleus and was the first comet to have its dust sampled and returned to Earth. Its surface is surprisingly rugged, with steep-walled depressions and flat-bottomed craters that suggest a complex geological structure. The comet is composed of ancient material that has remained largely frozen since the formation of the Solar System.

name: Comet 67P
description: Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko is a Jupiter-family comet that features a distinct 'rubber duck' shape with two large lobes connected by a neck. It has a very low density and is composed primarily of dust, water ice, and frozen gases like carbon dioxide. The comet's active surface produces spectacular jets of dust and gas as it approaches the heat of the Sun.

name: 4731 MonicaGrady
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Monica Grady, Emeritus Professor at the OU. Its official citation, written while she was curator of the meteorite collection at the Natural History Museum in London, reads: “Monica Grady (b. 1958), curator of the meteorite collection at the Natural History Museum in London, studies carbon isotopes in a wide range of meteorites with a focus on understanding the geologic processes leading to their formation. She is also actively involved in meteorite recovery efforts around the world.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20386 IanFranchi
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Ian Franchi, Emeritus Professor at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Ian Alan Franchi (b. 1961) is a British cosmochemist and emeritus professor at The Open University. He has forty years experience studying the origin and evolution of the early Solar System using advanced analytical techniques, and in particular, high-precision oxygen isotope measurements, on extraterrestrial materials.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20617 RichardGreenwood
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Richard Greenwood, a senior research fellow at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Richard Greenwood (b. 1957) is an English senior research fellow at The Open University who specializes in using oxygen isotopic analyses of extraterrestrial material to understand the origin and early evolution of the Solar System. He has also written a book on meteorites that was geared towards a general audience.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20626 Rider-Stokes
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Ben Rider-Stokes, a post-doctoral researcher at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Ben Gabriel Rider-Stokes (b. 1997) is an English post-doctoral researcher at The Open University specializing in understanding the timing of magmatic differentiation and volatile accretion of achondrites. He evaluates the spectral characteristics of meteorites in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared to identify meteoritic analogs for asteroids.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 25275 Jocelynbell
description: A main-belt asteroid named after astrophysicist Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Head of Physics at the OU from 1991 to 2001. Its official naming citation reads: “British astrophysicist Susan Jocelyn Bell Burnell (b. 1943) discovered the first radio pulsar in 1967 in collaboration with her thesis advisor, Anthony Hewish. In Aug. 2006 she presided over the IAU's adoption of resolutions defining the terms “planet” and “dwarf planet”.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 69423 OpenUni
description: A main-belt asteroid named after the OU itself. Its official naming citation reads: “The Open University (founded 1969 April 23) is the world’s leading university for flexible, innovative distance learning, having educated over 2 million part-time students. Through its research in astronomy, planetary and space science, the OU has a distinguished history of involvement in major Solar System exploration missions.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 10230 AndrewNorton
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Andrew Norton, formerly a Professor at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Andrew Norton (b. 1964) is an English astrophysicist at the Open University where he led major teaching and outreach initiatives, and carried out research into the time-domain astrophysics of compact binary stars. He led the SuperWASP Variable Stars citizen science project, supervised numerous Ph.D. students and won the RAS Higher Education Award.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 9831 SimonGreen
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Simon Green, Emeritus Professor at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Simon F. Green (b. 1959) has carried out observations of minor planets and transneptunian objects for over 20 years, starting with the use of the IRAS satellite to detect fast-moving objects.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 15614 Pillinger
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Colin Pillinger (1943-2014), Professor at the OU and principal investigator (PI) of the Beagle 2 Mars lander. Its official naming citation reads: “Colin T. Pillinger (b. 1943), a planetary geochemist, made significant discoveries in the light-element geochemistry of meteorites, diamonds, lunar samples and terrestrial samples. He is the originator and principal investigator of the Beagle 2 Mars lander. The name was suggested by E. K. Gibson.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20594 Pemartin
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Pierre-Etienne Martin, now a Postdoctoral Research Associate at the OU, for his earlier work. Its official naming citation reads: “Pierre-Etienne Martin (b. 1993) is a French planetary scientist at the University of Bern, investigating micron- to submicron-sized inclusions in Martian and carbonaceous meteorites. During his Ph.D., he studied refractory inclusions to assess aqueous alteration in CMs and joined the Hayabusa2 returned-samples analysis team.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 17920 Zarnecki
description: A main-belt asteroid named after space scientist John Zarnecki, formerly of the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “John C. Zarnecki (b. 1949), of the Open University, Milton Keynes, has developed spacecraft instrumentation to study the surfaces and atmospheres of planets, satellites and small bodies. He is a PI for the Huygens probe/lander on the Cassini mission to Saturn and Saturn VI (Titan).” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 3202 Graff
description: An outer main-belt asteroid of the Hilda group, named after Gareth (Graff) Vaughan Williams, who later did his PhD at the OU. It was named for his earlier work: working from Leighton Buzzard, England, he identified several low-numbered minor planets among objects that had been given provisional designations, and in 1990 he continued this work at the Minor Planet Center, correcting its files of old observations of low-numbered minor planets. The identification of this asteroid itself was made by C. M. Bardwell. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 9159 McDonnell
description: A main-belt asteroid named after J. A. M. (Tony) McDonnell, formerly Professor of Planetary and Space Sciences at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “J. A. M. (“Tony”) McDonnell (b. 1938) is recognised for his research on cosmic dust. With colleagues, he was the first to demonstrate the intact capture of space particulates in aerogel. He has flown instruments on a number of missions and has analysed impact craters on lunar samples and satellite surfaces exposed to space.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 158589 Snodgrass
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Colin Snodgrass, a research fellow at the OU from 2014 to 2018. Its official naming citation reads: “Colin Snodgrass (b. 1981) is an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory. His work centers on the characterization of inactive cometary nuclei through photometry, measuring their sizes, colors and rotation periods. He is also active in observing exoplanetary systems.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 15834 McBride
description: A main-belt asteroid on a steeply inclined orbit named after Neil McBride, formerly a lecturer at the OU and co-editor of its textbook An Introduction to the Solar System. Its official naming citation reads: “Neil McBride (b. 1966) has worked on many aspects of solar system dynamics, including meteor stream formation, interrelations between minor planets, comets and meteors, as well as the structure of the transneptunian region.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 8463 NaomiMurdoch
description: An outer main-belt asteroid named after Naomi Murdoch, who did her PhD at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Naomi Murdoch (b. 1984) completed her Ph.D. at The Open University, United Kingdom in 2012. Using microgravity flight experiments and numerical modeling, she investigated the behavior of granular material under minor-planet-like low-gravity surface conditions.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 11469 Rozitis
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Benjamin Rozitis, who did his PhD and postdoctoral research at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Benjamin Rozitis (b. 1984) is a research fellow at the Open University (UK) studying the physical and dynamical characterization of asteroid surfaces through spacecraft data, modeling, and microgravity experiments.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 30226 SamuelLeeJackson
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Samuel Lee Jackson, who did his PhD at the OU, observing asteroids with its PIRATE telescope in Tenerife. Its official naming citation reads: “Samuel Lee Jackson (b. 1997) is a British researcher at The Open University, Milton Keynes, UK, who specializes in observations of near-Earth asteroids and the use of small robotic telescopes.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 5497 SaraRussell
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Sara Russell, who did her PhD at the OU with Colin Pillinger and was later a Visiting Professor there. Its official naming citation reads: “As a researcher at the Natural History Museum in London, Sara Russell (b. 1966) studies the chemistry and mineralogy of meteorites to investigate the early solar system and origin of interstellar grains. She has collected meteorites in both hot and cold deserts and is principal editor of the Meteoritical Bulletin.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 6580 PhilBland
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Philip Bland, who was the OU’s curator of meteorites and did his PhD there. Its official naming citation reads: “Philip A. Bland (b. 1969), a research scientist at London's Imperial College, is involved in a variety of planetary and meteoritical studies. His fireball camera network offers an important glimpse into links between meteorites and minor planets.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 7552 Sephton
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Mark Sephton, who did his PhD at the OU and was a lecturer there from 2000 to 2005. Its official naming citation reads: “Mark A. Sephton (b. 1966) is a researcher in organic geochemistry and meteoritics at Imperial College, London. Through his research, he has determined new techniques for the analysis of organics in meteorites.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 7635 CarolineSmith
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Caroline Smith, who did her PhD at the OU. Its official naming citation reads: “Caroline Smith (b. 1976) the Head of Earth Sciences Collections and Principal Curator of Meteorites at the Natural History Museum in London. She studies mineralogy of meteorites, notably ureilites, to understand planetary processes, collected meteorites in Australia and has been principal editor of the Meteoritical Bulletin.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 42772 Kokotanekova
description: A main-belt asteroid named after Rosita Kokotanekova, who did her PhD at the OU on the nuclei of comets. Its official naming citation reads: “Rosita Kokotanekova (b. 1991) is a Research Fellow at ESO in Garching, Germany. She studies surface characteristics of comets, trans-Neptunian objects, and other small solar system bodies using ground-based photometry.” The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: Earth-Sun L1
description: Lagrange Point 1 is a point where the pull of the Sun and Earth balances a spacecraft's orbital motion, located approximately 1.5 million kilometres away from the Earth, directly between our planet and the Sun. It provides a constant, uninterrupted view of the Sun, making it the ideal location for solar monitoring satellites. Spacecraft at this point are essential for providing early warnings of solar flares and geomagnetic storms that could impact Earth.

name: Genesis
description: Genesis was a NASA mission that spent over two years at the Earth-Sun L1 point collecting samples of the solar wind to analyse the Sun's composition. It used specialised collector arrays to capture individual solar particles before returning them to Earth in a sample return capsule. Despite a hard landing in Utah, the mission successfully provided the first precise measurements of the Sun's oxygen and nitrogen isotopes.
ou_involvement: Our scientists were on the Genesis Science Team. We developed some of the collectors that captured the solar wind and new techniques to analyse the returned samples, and after the capsule’s crash landing we worked extensively to characterise and clean off the contamination. The contamination stopped us making meaningful measurements, but Genesis’s finding that the Sun is richer in oxygen-16 than the Earth, Moon, Mars and meteorites is a key reference point for our oxygen isotope research.

name: Ariel
description: Ariel is a planned ESA mission designed to perform the first large-scale survey of the chemical composition of exoplanet atmospheres. It will observe over a thousand diverse worlds in visible and infrared wavelengths to understand how planets form and evolve across the galaxy. The mission aims to find links between the atmospheres of planets and their parent stars and host environments.
ou_involvement: Our astronomers have served on Ariel’s science advisory team and led its working groups. Ariel will study the atmospheres of about 1,000 exoplanets, the first large survey of its kind, to show how planets form and evolve.

name: Open Science Observatories
description: The Open Science Observatories consist of two robotic telescopes, PIRATE and COAST, located at the Teide Observatory in Tenerife. They are designed to be operated remotely by students and researchers from anywhere in the world through a web-based interface. The facility is used for both undergraduate teaching and professional astronomical research, including the search for transiting exoplanets.
ou_involvement: We own and run these telescopes, a cornerstone of our distance-learning astronomy teaching. Our academics use them to monitor variable stars and to support space missions such as Ariel from the ground, and students use them to gain real experience of collecting and analysing astronomical data.

name: Mars Yard
description: The Mars Yard is a specialised planetary simulation facility located on the OU's campus in Milton Keynes, UK. It features a large area filled with regolith simulant and obstacles designed to mimic the challenging terrain found on the Martian surface. The site is used for autonomous rover testing, including navigation algorithms, and to train future planetary mission operators.
ou_involvement: Part of our teaching, the Mars Yard lets students drive robotic rovers across a simulated Martian landscape from their own homes, making space science hands-on for learners anywhere.

name: Robert Hooke Building
description: The OU's campus at Walton Hall, Milton Keynes, is home to its planetary and space science laboratories and to the teams who write its distance-learning courses. The OU’s mission is to be open to people, places, methods and ideas.
ou_involvement: Research in this visualisation feeds into our teaching. On our BSc Natural Sciences (Astronomy and Planetary Science), students take modules such as Astronomy (S284) and Planetary science and the search for life (S283, becoming Planetary science, S287, from October 2027), and on Remote experiments in physics and space (SXPS288) they run their own projects with our radio telescope in Milton Keynes or our PIRATE telescope in Tenerife. Postgraduates on our S818 Space Science module work with real mission data, such as Gaia’s.

crew.note: This resource would not exist without AI. Its content was largely written and reviewed by OU researchers, with LLMs helping to pull it all together and check it against published sources. The app itself was built in tandem with an LLM coding assistant, and some of the spacecraft and small-body models were made by a generative 3D AI from public reference images. People guided and checked every step.
